item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox have been home to some of baseball's most recognizable names, from early stars who helped shape the sport to modern legends who delivered on its biggest stage.
That history is reflected in The Sporting News 140: Baseball's Greatest Players, a project celebrating 140 of the greatest players in MLB history. The collection groups its selections into 14 distinct categories featuring 10 players, each connected by a common thread.
Leading off in July just after the All-Star break, the 14-week project included weekly drops and culminated with an unveiling of The Inner Circle, the 10 greatest of all-time, which included Ted Williams.
In all, 20 players with Red Sox ties earned spots on the list, representing generations of Boston baseball and a wide range of accomplishments.
Here is a closer look at the Red Sox legends featured in the project and what helped distinguish their careers.
(Editor's note: Player write-ups are courtesy of Paul Hembekides and Greg Thompson, co-authors of Baseball's Greatest Players.
Cy Young (1901-1908)
What is the most unbreakable record in major-league baseball history? You would be hard pressed to find a more compelling answer than the 511 wins collected by Denton True Young.
Cy Young led his league in walk rate (lowest) 14 times, most by any player in any major statistical category (pitching, hitting, or fielding).
Louis Van Oeyen/ WRHS / Getty Images
Pedro Martínez (1984-2004)
It was the apex of the steroid era, the most hitter-friendly environment in history, in which Pedro Martínez delivered the most dominant two-year run any pitcher ever has.
Through the 1998 season, only once had a pitcher struck out 10 hitters in seven consecutive games (1977 Nolan Ryan), a feat Pedro achieved twice in 1999. In 2000, Pedro became the first qualified pitcher to record twice as many strikeouts (284) as hits allowed (128) in a season.
WATCH: The Pedro Martinez collection, now streaming on NESN360
Mandatory Credit: Photo By Imagn Images
Tom Seaver (1986)
Known mostly for his dominance with the Mets, Seaver ended his career in Boston where he started 16 games at the age of 41.
“I would like to be a great artist,” Tom Seaver said. “I would quit pitching if I could paint like Monet or Rousseau. But I can't. What I can do is pitch, and I can do that very well.”
Tom Seaver is the all-time leader in career strikeouts (3,640) among those with a sub-3.00 ERA.
SN Archive (1986): Red Sox Finally Land Tom Seaver
SN
John Smoltz (2009)
John Smoltz fashioned two separate runs as a frontline starter, separated by a dominant three-year stretch as a closer after Tommy John surgery.
Like Seaver before him, you'd be forgiven for letting slip his fleeting time spent with the Sox. Smoltz pitched 708 games with the Braves, eight for the Red Sox and seven for the Cardinals.
John Smoltz won the 1996 NL Cy Young with a 24-win, 276-strikeout season, numbers not matched since Steve Carlton in 1980. Six years later, he finished third in Cy Young voting after recording the second-highest save total (55) in MLB history at the time.
Jimmie Foxx (1936-1942)
Blessed with unmatched strength that sent baseballs to places never before reached, Jimmie Foxx retired as the most prolific right-handed slugger in American League history.
Foxx collected 1,403 RBI in the 1930s, more than any player in any decade in MLB history.
Lefty Grove (1934-1941)
Lefty Grove’s sustained dominance renders him a compelling choice as the greatest left-handed pitcher of all time, a distinction history has rarely afforded him.
Grove pitched for 17 seasons and won nine ERA titles (5 with A’s, 4 with Red Sox); no other pitcher in MLB history has won more than seven.
Mookie Betts (2014-2019)
Mookie Betts has generated immense value in myriad ways on historically great teams, yet is rarely mentioned among the defining players of the 21st century.
Mookie Betts has collected 23.9 WAR on World Series-winning teams, most by any active player and most by any player since Derek Jeter's 29.9.
David Butler II-USA TODAY Sports Imagn Images
Wade Boggs (1982-1992)
Wade Boggs waited forever to be drafted, forever to reach the big leagues, and forever for baseball to admit how wrong it had been about him.
Boggs led the majors in times on base in seven consecutive seasons spanning 1983-89, the longest such streak all time.
RVR Photos-Imagn Images
Rickey Henderson (2002)
Rickey Henderson carried a swagger backed by his résumé: as baseball’s most prolific base stealer and run scorer, his case as the greatest leadoff hitter of all time is definitive.
Henderson recorded 1,406 stolen bases, 468 more than Lou Brock’s total; that 50% gap between first and second is the largest for any major counting statistic in major-league history.
David Ortiz (2003-2016)
David Ortiz met more moments than any player in Red Sox history, his knack for dramatics, potent bat and magnetic personality making him the face of the team’s curse-breaking renaissance.
Ortiz recorded three walkoffs in the 2004 postseason, the most by any player in a single postseason.
WATCH: The Big Papi collection, now streaming on NESN360
David Butler II-USA TODAY Sports Imagn Images
Curt Schilling (2004-2007)
Curt Schilling craved the spotlight and thrived under it, yet is better remembered for his post-career self-sabotage than for his big-game heroics.
Schilling started five postseason games with his team facing elimination and won all five, registering a 1.37 ERA while averaging eight innings and 112 pitches.
Robert Deutsch-Imagn Images
Tris Speaker (1907-1915)
Tris Speaker’s exploits were obscured by the omnipresent specter of Ty Cobb, the most celebrated American League player of the dead-ball era.
Speaker won AL MVP with Boston in 1912, the first player in franchise history to win the award, doing so in just its second year in existence.
Speaker totaled 1,131 extra-base hits against 393 strikeouts; that +738 margin is the largest in MLB history.
SN
Juan Marichal (1974)
Juan Marichal's baseball journey began in a Dominican farming village, bloomed in San Francisco where his unmistakable windup bedeviled hitters throughout the 1960s, and culminated with a plaque in Cooperstown.
A Pioneer in this collection of legends, its fitting that Marichal's one-year stint in Boston at the tail end of his HOF career paved the way for Seaver and Smoltz, among others, to follow suit.
Marichal's 191 wins, 197 complete games, 45 shutouts, and 55.3 WAR led all pitchers during the decade of the 1960s.
Adrian Beltré (2010)
A one-year, prove-it contract with Boston at 31 served as the prelude to Adrian Beltré’s improbable prime, which stretched deep into his thirties in Texas.
Beltré led the majors in defensive runs saved in the 15 seasons spanning 2003-17 (201), during which time only Albert Pujols and Miguel Cabrera accumulated more total bases than he did (4,132).
Dennis Wierzbicki-USA TODAY Sports Imagn Images
Carlton Fisk (1969, 1971-1980)
Carlton Fisk is remembered for willing one ball fair, but defined by the tenacity that kept him in the crouch until he was 45.
Fisk is the only catcher to compile 25 WAR on multiple teams (39.5 with Red Sox, 28.9 with White Sox).
Walter Iooss Jr./Sports Illustrated via Getty Images
Carl Yastrzemski (1961-1983)
Carl Yastrzemski arrived in Boston with the impossible task of replacing Ted Williams and retired 23 years later having become irreplaceable himself.
At Fenway Park, Yaz played 1,676 games, recorded 1,822 hits, and accumulated 1,063 RBI; each of those figures remain the most by any player in any stadium in MLB history.
Malcolm Emmons-USA TODAY Sports Imagn Images
Manny Ramirezv (2001-2008)
While we suspect many of Manny Ramirez’s contemporaries juiced, we know he did, and those two positive tests sealed his fate outside Cooperstown.
Ramirez, who debuted in 1993, owns the fourth-highest batting average (.312) among members of the 500-home run club; the average debut season of the top three is 1926 (Ted Williams, Babe Ruth, Jimmie Foxx).
Roger Clemens (1984-1996)
Roger Clemens fought to clear his name in court and won, but the most accomplished pitcher in history was never acquitted in the court of public opinion.
Clemens went 18 years between his first (1986) and last (2004) Cy Young; that is seven years longer than the next-longest gap of its kind (Justin Verlander: 11 (2011, 2022)).
RVR Photos-USA TODAY Sports Imagn Images
Ted Williams (1939-1942, 1946-1960)
Ted Williams was to hitting what Albert Einstein was to physics -- an obsessive, unrelenting mad scientist whose genius was generations ahead of its time.
Williams posted a .500 on-base percentage across a 1,068-game span between 1940 and 1951, comprising 47% of his career.
Babe Ruth (1914-1919)
Baseball history can be cleanly divided into two acts - before Babe Ruth picked up a bat and after he turned the home run into its most valuable currency and grandest spectacle.
Ruth hit 54 home runs in 1920, outhomering every other team in the American League; his total comprised 14.6% of the league’s total output.
Detroit Free Press - Imagn Images
A lasting Boston legacy
The Red Sox's representation in the Sporting News project reflects the franchise's place across multiple eras of baseball history. Some of these players became synonymous with Boston, while others spent only part of their careers in a Red Sox uniform.
Their accomplishments span power hitting, pitching dominance, defensive excellence and postseason heroics. Together, they illustrate how Boston's baseball history connects to the broader story of the sport.
The full Sporting News collection, The 140 Greatest Baseball Players, is available here.

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies hit two clutch home runs during Game 2 of the NL Wild Card, with Kyle Schwarber and Bryce Harper going back-to-back to tie the game up late.
But with the game in extra innings, the Phillies got an incredibly clutch solo homer to right field from Alec Bohm to put the Phillies up 4-3. That extra-inning, go-ahead HR from Bohm made some incredible MLB history.
According to Jayson Stark of The Athletic, Bohm's homer has made him the third player ever to hit a go-ahead home run in extra innings in an elimination game during the postseason, joining David Ortiz and Carlton Fisk.
Alec Bohm joins David Ortiz, Carlton Fisk with all-time clutch HR
"Tie-breaking extra-inning HR by cleanup hitters in postseason elimination game: Carlton Fisk, 1975, WS Game 6; David Ortiz, 2004, ALCS Game 4; Alec Bohm, 2026, WSC Game 2," Stark shared.
There is no other player in MLB history other than these three hitters to have a go-ahead home run in extra innings when their team was facing elimination.
This incredibly clutch homer kept the Phillies' season alive, and it has now made Bohm a part of some of the most iconic home runs in MLB postseason history.
Although it doesn't feel like it at all right now, this homer from Bohm is in some very rare air, with Fisk's '75 homer and Ortiz's '04 homer two of the most legendary in MLB history.
If the Phillies can go on a run to win the 2026 World Series, this Bohm home run will be the moment that sparked this Phillies team to greatness.
But even if the Phillies don't win it all, Bohm's clutch home run is still one of the craziest of all time. On the brink of elimination, Bohm hit a clutch homer in extra innings to save the season. It doesn't get a whole lot better than that.

item.content:encoded:
A Red Sox vs. Yankees ticket stub from May 31, 1976, was Concord Historical Society volunteer Bill Kretovic’s favorite item from a time capsule buried at Rundlett Middle School.
The game took place just 11 days after the famous bench-clearing brawl between the Red Sox and Yankees when Boston catcher Carlton Fisk tagged out Yankee outfielder Lou Piniella. Tensions were still high as angry Red Sox fans threw debris and exploded firecrackers at the Yankees players.
The red, white and blue stub, partially ripped on the bottom, still displays the date and price of the game — $5. Kretovic found an old retainer buried alongside the ticket. While less historically significant, it still intrigued him.
“I think of that as like someone coming home from school that day and going, ‘I lost my retainer, Mom!’ And it’s actually in the time capsule,” Kretovic said.
Dozens of artifacts, including the ticket and the retainer, sprawled across tables inside a basement storage area in Rundlett Middle School. The items were found in two containers buried in the middle school’s courtyard back when it was a junior high school. On Sept. 11, Kretovic dug up the time capsules and has since been drying and researching the items inside.
“Throughout this process, it’s kind of funny, because I really kind of have a little bit of like, ‘Am I Indiana Jones? Am I Marty McFly in ‘Back to the Future?'” Kretovic said. “I come down here, and that stuff is 30 years old; this stuff is 50 years old. Then, I go back upstairs, and it’s 2026.”
Alumni get a first look
On Friday, the Concord High School Class of 1976 gathered for its 50-year reunion. As part of their tour, alumni got the first look at the newly recovered artifacts.
“While this stuff is technically not theirs, they may have information as to where maybe their time capsule is,” Kretovic said. “But it’s from their era. And I think they can see and they can go, ‘Okay, yep, saddle shoes, we all wore those.'”
In addition to the 1976 artifacts, visiting alumni got to see items from the time capsule buried in 1992 by the class of 1995. The four trash bins that made up the capsule were uncovered in June.
The 1992 capsule contained VCRs, a cassette tape, Nintendo games, Rolling Stone magazines, a class schedule and pop culture items.
Cathy Dawson and her husband, Michael Painter, came up from Florida to join the reunion.
“It’s amazing and fun, I mean, just to think, ‘Wow, 50 years ago, they buried it,'” Painter said.
His wife completed his thought: “And just remembering it now and to have it on our 50th high school reunion, too, it really just makes it special,” she said.
Painter said the tour reminded him of how simple life was back then.
“I’ll be looking forward to what they got 50 years from now,” Painter said.
Finding the 1976 time capsule
Nathan Amsden carefully drew a map to his class time capsule in June 1976. Next to an arrow pointing to the time capsule, Amsden wrote, “To be opened in June, 2004.”
Kretovic used this map, the Pythagorean Theorem and his tape measure to find the marked spot and dig over the course of two days.
“We weren’t really sure what material it was made out of,” Kretovic said. “So, if it was metal, it could have been rusted away. If it was wood, it could have been rotted away. Just had no idea.”
As he dug, Kretovic maneuvered around some metal plates and the large root of a nearby tree, planted after the time capsule was buried.
“As I was doing that, I was about ready to call it quits, because I said, ‘I’m down this far, I don’t know if it’s gone, if someone already found it'” Kretovic said. “So, as I’m digging some of the dirt out and tossing it up onto the piles over here, I notice that piece of plastic.”
That plastic was the top of two hard plastic barrels: the 1976 time capsules.
After finding the containers, Kretovic walked middle school students through the process of how he found the spot using the map.
“We asked them how old their parents were, and one girl said, ‘Oh, 39!’ I’m like, okay, how old are your grandparents?” Kretovic said.
Having located, unearthed, restored and researched many of the artifacts, Kretovic asked himself, ‘What does this all mean?’
“There was some thought going into what we’re putting in here for people to see, in this case, 30 years from now,” Kretovic said, pointing to some of the items buried in 1992. “What we had on our minds and what was going on.”
The 1976 and 1992 time capsules are not alone.
One buried in 1989 by the class of 1992 has been located, but is paved over and will be dug up later. Another, created in 1988 by the class of 1991 was never buried and is not yet opened.
The hunt for time capsules started when Rundlett librarian Regina Wall told Principal Jay Richard she wanted to create another time capsule to mark the new building. Richard then remembered a box he found when he arrived at Rundlett. It contained envelopes with hand-drawn maps from students showing where their time capsule was buried.
Since then, Richard has contacted alumni and sought the help of the historical society to find and uncover past time capsules as construction continues for the new middle school.
As the middle school considers creating another time capsule, Kretovic recommends an above-ground model.
When he opened up the 1992 bins, Kretovic discovered each bin had three plastic liners with items put in multiple bags and sealed inside Ziplocs as well.
Despite that effort, Kretovic said some of the bags were like fishbowls that he had to pop and drain out. Many of the items sustained water damage. To ensure items are preserved going forward, he suggested a room inside the new school with drawers to store artifacts for each year.
As of now, Kretovic said he is not sure what will happen to the items recovered from the time capsules, but he plans to support Richard with what he and the school choose to do.

item.content:encoded:
On the edge of the wind-scoured Salt Lake Valley, between rows of gray and white houses and sunbaked driveways, you can find a little taste of Fenway Park.
A housing subdivision in Herriman, Utah, is turning heads online for its streets, each of which bears the name of a Red Sox star from the annals of team history: Pesky Lane, Pedroia Street, and Varitek Drive, to name a few.
The names, which could be ripped straight from the banners on Van Ness Street, stand out in a place like Herriman, a Salt Lake City suburb 500 miles from the nearest Major League Baseball stadium. There’s little else to suggest Copper Fields, a neat grid of roughly 200 houses completed by Edge Homes in 2024, has a link to Boston.
But once social media caught wind of the Sox-heavy ‘hood over the weekend, fans were ablaze with speculation.
“Ready to blow my savings and move to Utah so I can live on Pedroia Street,” one commenter wrote on X, posting an image of a three-bed, three-bath home on sale for $669,000 (slightly cheaper than a 700-square-foot condo in the South End).
“[I don’t care] about getting priced out of Boston,” opined Anna Caruso of Section 10, a Red Sox podcast, beneath a photo of the development. “You’ll find me here.”
Another commenter said that, in person, the neighborhood is “brand-new and pretty nice,” though “all of the houses look basically the same.”
“I wonder what [percentage] of families that live here have no idea what the streets mean,” they added.
So, who’s behind all these names? There’s not much of a Red Sox connection in the area to speak of, aside from the fact that a young David Ortiz played with Salt Lake’s minor league team while still a Minnesota Twins prospect.
But that didn’t matter to Brandon Parr, the Edge Homes project manager who selected the names. Parr, 47, was born and raised in Utah — but he lives and breathes the Red Sox all the same.
“I liked Wade Boggs a lot, and he just happened to play for them, so I became a fan,” he said. “The rest is history.”
When Parr got the chance to name an entire new subdivision, his vision was clear.
“I don’t think anybody on my team really knew what I was doing until they saw the first flat be recorded [on the master plan],” he said.
Parr made sure to include a (Wade) Boggs Way, as well as a (Jerry) Remy Road, named after the late broadcaster and former player, and a Xander (Bogaerts) Lane. The neighborhood even has a Yawkey Way, named after the controversial Red Sox owner whose name once marked what is now Jersey Street. (Edge Homes seems to have missed the memo on that one.)
Plenty of fans online wondered why Parr didn’t nod toward other Red Sox legends. The answer, he said, was that some names were hard to get local approval for. Ted Williams, for example, had a surname common enough that there’s already a Camp Williams Road in town.
“Some of them are personal favorites,” Parr said of the player names. “I was a big fan of Nathan Eovaldi and his performance in 2018, so he’s on there. ... Boggs was the reason I started liking the Red Sox, so I had to get him. I was just trying to pick some names that meant something to me, and to the organization as well.”
It’s not the first time Parr has gotten creative with street names. Edge Homes takes on anywhere from 10 to 12 development projects a year, and naming all those streets can be “a little bit of a daunting task sometimes,” he said.
Aside from Red Sox players, Parr has also referenced comic book movie actors. A subdivision in Riverton, Utah, includes a Hemsworth Lane and a Hiddleston Drive, named after Chris Hemsworth and Tom Hiddleston, the actors who play Thor and Loki in Marvel films.
“My company encourages us to be creative,” he said. “It’s just something fun that we do as a team.”
Parr, who carries a Red Sox water bottle and owns a replica championship ring, has taken his family to a few games at Fenway. But he admits that Red Sox fans aren’t exactly plentiful in Salt Lake City.
“I’m kind of alone,” he said. “At the office, I would say there’s definitely more Yankees fans around me than Red Sox fans. But I’ll be a Red Sox fan till the day I die.”
At least one Herriman resident recognizes the significance of the street names.
Chris Watson, 56, a graphic designer and photographer, has lived in Utah for over two decades. But he was raised in Framingham, collecting Red Sox trading cards and watching Luis Tiant and Jim Rice and Carl Yastrzemski.
“I don’t keep up with [the team] as much anymore,” he said. “But the only baseball hat I’ll wear is a Red Sox hat.”
When he was searching for a place to build a new home a few years back, he realized “really quickly” the names on the lot were something special.
It was a “really fun coincidence” to end up living on Fisk Road — named after Carlton Fisk, Watson’s favorite player on the (in)famous 1978 team. Even that team, lamented for its end-of-season collapse against the Yankees, still holds a special place in his heart.
“That was the peak of fandom for my 8, 9-year old self,” he said. “He would have thought it was really cool [to be living here].”
Camilo Fonseca can be reached at camilo.fonseca@globe.com. Follow him on X @fonseca_esq and on Instagram @camilo_fonseca.reports.
